questions.problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y=\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}}+\frac{x}{2}$ at the point $(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{4}).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}}+\frac{x}{2}.$ Computing the derivative ${f}^{′}(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}}+\frac{x}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-3}+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute ${f}^{′}(-\frac{1}{2}),$ which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(-\frac{1}{2})=-\frac{1}{2}\cdot {(-\frac{1}{2})}^{-3}+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{2}{9}.
$$

questions.problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y=2{x}^{3}-7x$ at the point $(-1,5).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=2{x}^{3}-7x.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}-7x)=6{x}^{2}-7\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(-1,5):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(-1)=6(-1)^{2}-7=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(-1)}=1.
$$

questions.problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y=2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}-2{x}^{2}$ at the point $(1,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}-2{x}^{2}.$ Computing the derivative ${f}^{′}(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}-2{x}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3/2}-2{x}^{2}) \\  & =3{x}^{1/2}-4x.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute ${f}^{′}(1)$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1)=3(1)^{1/2}-4(1)=-1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=1.
$$

questions.problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=\frac{3}{{x}^{3}}$ at the point $(1,3)$ is given by $x+py=q$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Find the value of $p-q.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=\frac{3}{{x}^{3}}.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{3}{{x}^{3}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{-3}) \\  & =-9{x}^{-4} \\  & =-\frac{9}{{x}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1)=-\frac{9}{(1)^{4}}=-9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=\frac{1}{9}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(3) & =\frac{1}{9}(x-1) \\ 9y-27 & =x-1 \\ x-9y & =-26.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p-q=-9-(-26)=17.$

questions.problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x)=3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}$ at the point $(8,12)$ intersects the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{2/3}) \\  & =2{x}^{-1/3} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt[3]{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(8)=\frac{2}{\sqrt[3]{8}}=1,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-1.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-12 & =-(x-8) \\ y & =-x+8+12 \\ y & =20-x.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $y$-axis by setting $x=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =20-0 \\ y & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $y$-axis at  $(0,20).$

Taking the derivative, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3})=3{x}^{2}.
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(1)=3(1)^{2}=3,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =-\frac{1}{3}(x-(1)) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{1}{3}+1 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{4}{3} & =0 \\ \frac{1}{3}x & =\frac{4}{3} \\ x & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(\,4,0\,).$

                    Calculating the Slope of a Normal Line to a Curve at a Point
canonical_examples.problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y = 2x^3 -x^2$ at the point $(1,1).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $f(x) = 2x^3-x^2.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
f'(x)  =6x^2 -2x
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
m=f'(1) = 6(1)^2 - 2(1) = 4
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line $m'$ is

$$
m' = -\dfrac{1}{m} = -\dfrac 1 4.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=x^3 - x^2$ at the point $(1,0)$ is given by $y=px+q$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Find the values of $p$ and $q.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=x^3 - x^2.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}-{x}^{2})=3{x}^{2}-2x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1, 0){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1)=3-2=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line $m'$ is

$$
m'=-\dfrac{1}{m}=-1.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-0 & =-(x-1) \\ y & =-x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=-1$ and $q=1.$

Example: 
                    Determining the Intercepts of a Normal Line
canonical_examples.problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x) = 2\sqrt{x} -4x$ at the point $(1,-2)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{x}-4x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{1/2}-4x) \\  & ={x}^{-1/2}-4.\end{aligned}
$$

     

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m=f'(1) = (1)^{-1/2} - 4 = -3,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
m' = -\dfrac{1}{m} = \dfrac 1 3.
$$

The equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(-2) & =\frac{1}{3}(x-1) \\ y+2 & =\frac{1}{3}(x-1) \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{1}{3}-2 \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{7}{3} & =0 \\ \frac{1}{3}x & =\frac{7}{3} \\ x & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(7,0).$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The equation of the normal line to the curve $y = f(x)$ at the point $P(x_1,y_1),$ in point-slope form, is given by

$$
y - y_1 = m (x - x_1), \hspace{1cm} m=-\dfrac{1}{f'(x_1)}.
$$

Here, $m=-\dfrac{1}{f'(x_1)}$ because the slope of the normal line is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line, and $f'(x_1)$ represents the slope of the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ at the point $(x_1,y_1).$

For example, suppose we want to compute the equation of the normal line to the curve $y=x^2$ at the point $A(1,1).$ This normal line is the dashed line shown below, which is perpendicular to the solid tangent line. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14212989/assets/31ba09ff14e5bd485794f283c5d6a5b087b6c21fdb9242af01b75ec8e8744e0d.png)

Since $y=x^2,$ we have $f(x)=x^2.$ We begin by calculating the derivative of $f(x)\mathbin{:}$

$$
f'(x) 		 = \dfrac {\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(x^2)= 2x
$$

At $A(1,1),$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
f'(1) 	= 2(1) = 2.
$$

However, we want the normal line, and the slope of the normal line is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
m = -\dfrac{1}{f'(1)} = -\dfrac{1}{2}
$$

 

Finally, we work out the equation of the normal line using the point-slope form:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =-\frac{1}{2}(x-1) \\ y & =-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{1}{2}+1 \\ y & =-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the normal line is $y=-\dfrac x 2 + \dfrac 3 2.$ We could also write this in standard form as $x+2y=3.$
